one_liner: Safe-Rust, ABI-identical rewrite of picohttpparser; beats scalar -O2 C only on header-heavy requests, loses on six of eight workloads.
what_it_does: A reimplementation of h2o/picohttpparser (pinned at f4d94b48, which is also upstream HEAD) that exports the same five C symbols (phr_parse_request, phr_parse_response, phr_parse_headers, phr_decode_chunked, phr_decode_chunked_is_in_data) with the same struct layouts. You build it as a cdylib or staticlib and link it under the unchanged upstream picohttpparser.h. It is zero-copy: output pointers point into your buffer, and nothing is allocated per parse. The author checked it against the C original on 133,352 differential cases (return value, pointers, lengths and chunked-decoder state) with 0 mismatches, and the unmodified upstream test.c passes 8/8 against it.
how_it_is_fast: It is only faster on long header values, where get_token_to_eol runs a SWAR prescan: it loads 16 bytes as two u64 words, tests all 8 lanes of each word at once for any byte outside 0x20..0x7E, skips clean blocks and drops to the exact per-byte loop on a dirty one. C's scalar path (built without SSE4.2) checks one byte at a time in an 8x unrolled loop, so the SWAR scan wins on long runs of printable ASCII; the other change is a 256-entry tchar lookup table (measured ~11% faster than without it). The parser core has no unsafe code and uses bounds-checked .get() reads. Each export pays for catch_unwind, and in the benchmark each call also went through a DLL import hop; that fixed cost is why tiny and reject-fast inputs are slower.
when_to_use: You link picohttpparser from C (or through FFI) and want a memory-safe parser behind the exact same ABI and behavior, with no changes at the call sites.
Requests with many long, plain-ASCII header values (the 64 headers x 64 B, ~4.9 KB case): ~828 vs ~1,218 ns/parse against -O2 scalar C (0.68 ratio). It still led at -O3 (0.82).
Header blocks like upstream bench.c's ~620 B / 11-header request, when your C build has no SSE4.2: ~166 vs ~201 ns/parse (0.83).

You want hardened failure on caller contract violations. Null outputs, last_len > len, or a corrupted chunked-decoder state give a defined -1/-2 instead of a segfault, an out-of-bounds read or a hang.
when_not_to_use: Speed is the goal and your picohttpparser is built with SSE4.2/-march=native. In the native tier (bench.c request), C with pcmpestri was 1.45x faster than Rust (~138 vs ~200 ns/parse). This was recorded at an earlier revision (935b176), before the 16-byte SWAR change, and never re-run.
Small or typical traffic: Rust was slower on tiny 37 B requests (1.48x), ~400 B requests (1.10x), ~150 B responses (1.18x) and 38 B chunked bodies (1.20x).
Reject-fast / DoS-filter paths: rejecting at byte 1 takes 1.81x as long (~5.7 vs ~3.1 ns). At opt-level=3 the Rust malformed path gets 1.68x worse, and the cause is still open.

You need production maturity. The code was written in about a day (2026-09-08/09). There is one author, 2 stars, no CI, no tags and no crates.io release. It was built and tested only on one Windows machine with rustc 1.96.1. No real consumer (H2O/Plack/Furl) has been integrated, only a loopback TCP harness and a ctypes harness.
Rust callers who want an idiomatic API: the only public interface is the unsafe extern "C" functions plus the repr structs, and the safe core modules are private.

integration.form: crate (cdylib + staticlib + rlib); not on crates.io, build from git
integration.min_toolchain: Rust edition 2024 (rust-version = 1.85 is a declared floor only; only rustc 1.96.1 was ever run)
integration.platforms: Portable Rust with no arch intrinsics or SIMD. Layout asserts only on 64-bit targets. Tested only on Windows x86-64 (i5-12400F); 32-bit and non-Windows builds are not exercised.
integration.thread_safety: Not stated explicitly. The parse functions are stateless and write only to caller-owned outputs, and the only static is an immutable lookup table. Chunked-decoder state lives in a caller-owned struct (one per stream), as in upstream.
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial: same 5 symbols, header and struct layout, and matches C on all 133,352 differential cases. It deliberately differs on 4 contract-violation inputs (D001-D004: returns -1/-2/0 where C faults, reads out of bounds or hangs). It has no SSE4.2 fast path.

gotchas: The README's 'segfault' framing is about caller contract violations: null pointers, last_len > len, a forged decoder _state, and a NULL is_in_data query. Differential fuzzing of hostile bytes (~1.94M executions) recorded 0 crashes on either side.
Memory safety stops at the FFI seam. Each export builds a slice with slice::from_raw_parts(buf, len), so a wrong (buf, len) from the caller is still undefined behavior, exactly as in C.

Keep the pinned release profile (opt-level=2, LTO, codegen-units=1, overflow-checks off, panic=unwind). Raising opt-level to 3 regressed the malformed path 1.68x. A panic inside a parser is caught at the seam and returned as -1.
Every published Rust number came through the DLL, because MinGW ld could not link the MSVC-built staticlib. Rust callers linking the rlib get cross-crate inlining and will see different numbers.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: The vkrasnov AVX2 fork (1.68-1.79x), httpp (~2.26x at -O3) and hparse (~12.5% wall-clock) are all reported faster than picohttpparser overall, while this one wins only on header-heavy inputs against scalar -O2 C. Pick it when you want memory-safe code behind picohttpparser's exact ABI and behavior; pick a sibling when speed is the goal.
verified_claims_summary: One same-session, interleaved whole-loop timer run on a single i5-12400F under Windows compared the Rust cdylib (rustc 1.96.1, opt-level=2, LTO, CGU1) with picohttpparser f4d94b48 built by GCC 16.2.0 at -O2 (no SSE4.2, asserts live): Rust was faster on the 64x64 B-header request (0.68) and on the bench.c ~620 B request (0.83), and slower on typical (1.10), response (1.18), chunked (1.20), tiny (1.48) and malformed (1.81), with streaming at parity (1.02). Six of the eight rows are flagged for >5% trial spread, and against -O3 -march=native C at an older revision the bench.c request flips to C 1.45x faster.
status_note: Active but brand-new (created 2026-09-09; the last commit, 2026-09-11, was README-only), single-author, MIT and 1,527 lines with no dependencies, so it is easy to vendor, though it has no releases or CI and its author presents it as a correctness and safety experiment, not a speed claim.
